Postdoctoral research fellow 'Computational neurophysiology of human motivation'We are looking for a postdoctoral researcher with expertise and interest in the computational neuroscience of human motivation and cognitive control. The goal of the project is to unravel the neurophysiological signatures of value-based decision making and controllability.The project will involve experimental design, data acquisition, and advanced statistical and computational modeling of neurophysiological (iEEG, single-neuron activity and local field potentials from micro-electrode recordings) and behavioral data from human volunteers and clinical patients.You will play a key role in the ERC Advanced CHEMCONTROL team, led by Roshan Cools, at Donders which comprises research master students, research assistants, 2 PhD students and a senior postdoc. The CHEMCONTROL team will integrate computational modeling, human neurophysiology, pharmacological fMRI, chemical PET imaging, and focused transcranial ultrasound stimulation to unravel the brain mechanisms by which we adapt flexibly to the threats and opportunities around us.You are expected to have the background knowledge, skills and motivation that will allow you to fully exploit and learn from the rich research environment that the Donders Institute provides (including its intellectual and technical infrastructure). You are an independent scholar and brain scientist with quantitative skills and expertise in the domain of human motivation, decision making, learning, and cognitive control. You are ready to acquire the skills required for conducting all phases of computational neuroimaging and neurophysiology, including conceptual and experimental design, computational modeling of behavior, data acquisition, data analysis, data interpretation and publication. You are also expected to be a team player, willing and able to work closely with multiple research group leaders, postdocs, fellows PhD students, research assistants and research master students.You have a passion for mechanistic research at the interface of neurophysiology, computational cognitive science, and decision neuroscience. You are curious, ambitious, and can work independently. Your English is fluent in speaking and writing at an academic level. Speaking Dutch is not required for this position.You also meet the following requirements:You hold or have finished and nearly obtained a PhD in the field of computational cognitive neuroscience, biomedical engineering, or a related field;You have experience and skills in neurophysiological data analyses;You have experience with, or are interested in, computational and statistical modelling of behavioral data;You have excellent programming skills and a strong quantitative background.This position requires a Certificate of Conduct (VOG).

Ultrasound and tomosynthesis are the most prevalent modalities used for breast imaging, and each has its specific advantages and disadvantages. Ultrasound uses sound waves to create a cross-sectional image of the tissue and has excellent depth resolution, but limited resolution in directions perpendicular to the transmitted ultrasound lines. Tomosynthesis uses x rays to create a pseudo-3D representation of the breast with high in-plane spatial resolution, but low out-of-plane (depth) resolution. Therefore, both techniques are complementary to each other.We plan to develop a joint system that will use the information from each modality to improve the image quality of the other, yielding not only a multi-modality imaging system, but a joint imaging system. The combination of tomosynthesis and ultrasound into a single joint imaging system will yield improved images from two independent and complementary sources, with inherent spatial correlation, allowing for improved lesion detection, even in dense breasts, and the direct multi-modal assessment of suspicious lesions. For this multi-disciplinary project, we will be working in collaboration with the Advanced X-ray Tomography Imaging (AXTI) lab of our Department, who will be developing the X-ray aspects of this system (see accompanying vacancy).In this project, you will focus on 3D ultrasound by using an ultra-wide ultrasound transducer that is mounted in a paddle required for acquisition of tomosynthesis data. In this way, a 3D ultrasound dataset can be acquired that can be used to improve the x-ray data by using the high-axial resolution US data. Additionally, the ultrasound data can be improved by using the high-resolution x-ray data. You will develop and validate these methods using both digital and physical phantoms, working towards first patient images at the end of the project. All of this will be in collaboration with a PhD student focusing on the x-ray aspects of the project, and industry partners to facilitate the translation of these methods into clinical evaluation. Tasks will also include presenting at international scientific conferences and writing papers on the newly developed methods and study results.RequirementsYou should be a creative and enthusiastic researcher with a MSc degree in physics, mathematics, engineering, Technical medicine, or similar.Experience or interest in physics modeling, inverse problems, and/or image processing, and affinity with biomedical research.Experience in programming in python, C/C++, Matlab, or similar.Excellent communication skills in English, both written and spoken.Good to knowThe following should be included in your application: CV, letters of motivation, list of completed courses and grades, and reprints or, preferably, links to your thesis or any scientific publications or reports that you have written.The first job interviews will take place in November 2026. Please take this into account.
